Use the catalogue to compare the current products and kit options. For a complete farm price, share the plot size, crop, water source and location so the bill of materials is sized instead of guessed.

sections.heading: Gravity-fed or pumped: how water pressure changes the kit
paragraphs: Roughly ten metres of water head gives one bar of pressure. Thin-wall drip tape often works at low pressure, so a small plot can run from a tank on a raised stand, while a larger field or long laterals usually needs a pump to keep flow even from the first emitter to the last.

Pressure also decides the filter. A screen filter is common on low-pressure gravity systems; disc filters suit pumped systems and dirtier water. Water from a dam or river usually needs more filtration than borehole or tank water, which changes both the price and the maintenance routine.

sections.heading: How many drip lines per bed?
paragraphs: Common practice is two lines per bed for widely spaced crops such as tomatoes and capsicum, and three or four lines for closely planted crops such as onions and garlic. More lines per bed means more dripline, more fittings and a higher flow demand, so it raises the kit price and can lower pressure at the end of the run.
Treat this as a starting point. Bed width, soil type and the planting pattern you use should confirm the final layout.

Do I need a pump? Not always. It depends on the height of your tank, the length of the laterals and the size of the plot. Share those details and DripTech can recommend gravity or pumped supply.

title: Drip Tape vs Dripline in Kenya: Buying Guide | DripTech
description: Compare drip tape and dripline for Kenyan farms: wall thickness, emitter spacing, durability, filtration and pressure, and how to choose for your crop.
h1: Drip tape vs dripline: which is right for your farm?
intro: Drip tape and dripline both deliver water near crop roots, but they are not interchangeable in every field. The better choice depends on crop spacing, season length, pressure, filtration, installation method and how often the lines will be moved.

sections.heading: What is drip tape?
paragraphs: Drip tape is generally a thin-walled irrigation tube designed for row crops and planned seasonal use. It can be a practical option where lines are laid out in crop beds and operating pressure stays within the product specification.
Tape products differ in wall thickness, emitter spacing, flow rate and pressure limits. Check the manufacturer's data rather than assuming every tape roll has the same performance or service life.

sections.heading: What is dripline?
paragraphs: Dripline is a broad term for tubing used in drip irrigation; many products have built-in emitters and are available in different wall thicknesses and emitter designs. Some are intended for repeated or longer-term installation, but actual durability depends on the specific product and operating conditions.

For orchards, greenhouses and vegetable rows, compare the emitter type, spacing, flow rate, tube diameter, pressure range and compatibility with the proposed layout. The label alone does not tell you whether a product is suitable.

sections.heading: Compare the specifications before buying
bullets: Wall thickness and stated service conditions
Emitter spacing and discharge rate per emitter or metre
Recommended operating pressure and allowable pressure variation
Filtration requirements for the water source
Tube diameter, connectors, end fittings and flushing method
UV exposure, handling, storage and whether lines will be reused
Supplier warranty and availability of matching repair fittings

sections.heading: Which option suits different farms?
paragraphs: For short-season row crops, a suitable thin-wall tape may meet the design need when the layout, water quality and pressure are controlled. For repeated use or installations where lines remain in place, compare thicker-wall dripline products and their manufacturer specifications.

For orchards or widely spaced plants, individual emitters or a purpose-designed dripline layout may be more appropriate than choosing tape solely because it is cheaper per roll. The required number of lines per row depends on root-zone coverage, soil, crop stage and irrigation design.

sections.heading: Filtration, pressure and maintenance matter
paragraphs: Both tape and dripline can clog if the water contains particles, algae or other material that the filtration system does not remove. Select filtration according to the water source and emitter specifications, then maintain and flush the system as directed.

Too much or too little pressure can create uneven application or damage components. Use the manufacturer's pressure range and check the actual flow and pressure under operating conditions before expanding the system.

sections.heading: How to choose the right product in Kenya
paragraphs: Before requesting a quotation, note your crop, planted area, row and plant spacing, water source, available flow, elevation changes and whether the system is seasonal or permanent. Share product labels or photos if you are comparing two rolls.
DripTech Eco Flow can help discuss available irrigation components and the information needed for a farm-specific quotation. Confirm current stock, specifications and prices before ordering.

title: Why Drip Irrigation Emitters Get Blocked | Filter & Flushing Guide
description: Troubleshoot blocked drip emitters in Kenya: water quality, filter selection, flushing, pressure checks and practical prevention.
h1: Why drip irrigation emitters get blocked
intro: Uneven watering or emitters that stop flowing can be caused by suspended particles, mineral deposits, biological growth, damaged lines or poor system operation. Diagnose the cause before replacing parts.

sections.heading: Start with the water and the filter
paragraphs: Inspect the water source and filter before opening every lateral. Sand, algae, organic matter and fine particles can reach emitters when filtration is unsuitable, damaged or overdue for cleaning.

The correct filter depends on the water source, emitter passage specification and system flow. A filter that is too coarse may allow particles through; one that is too restrictive or dirty can reduce pressure.

sections.heading: A safe troubleshooting sequence
bullets: Check whether the problem affects one lateral, one zone or the whole system.
Read pressure before and after the filter if gauges are installed; a large difference can indicate a dirty filter.
Shut the system down safely and clean the filter according to its manufacturer's instructions.
Flush accessible line ends into a suitable drain area, following the system design.
Inspect a sample of emitters and connectors for damage or deposits; replace damaged components rather than forcing them open.
Restart and check whether flow and pressure are more uniform.

sections.heading: Prevent repeat blockages
paragraphs: Use water-source-appropriate filtration, routine filter cleaning, planned flushing and compatible fertigation practices. Keep chemical treatment decisions specific to the water analysis and product instructions; do not mix treatment chemicals casually.
Record filter cleaning, pressure readings and affected zones. A repeated pattern helps identify whether the source is filtration, hydraulics or damaged equipment.

sections.heading: Equipment to inspect or replace
bullets: Screen or disc filters matched to the system
Filter mesh specification and spare elements
Flush valves and end caps
Pressure gauges and regulators
Compatible dripline connectors and replacement laterals

sections.heading: When to request technical help

description: Understand low irrigation pump pressure: suction leaks, blocked filters, pipe losses, pump sizing and practical checks before replacing equipment.
h1: Why an irrigation pump has low pressure
intro: Low pressure can originate at the water source, suction pipe, filter, pump, delivery pipe or irrigation zone. Check the whole system rather than assuming the pump itself has failed.

sections.heading: Common causes to investigate
bullets: Water level too low or source flow insufficient
Air entering the suction line or a suction connection leaking
Blocked strainer or filter restricting flow
Pipe diameter too small or long pipe runs causing friction losses
Too many zones or sprinklers operating together
Pump operating outside its intended flow and head range
Worn components or electrical supply issues requiring qualified service

sections.heading: Check the system in order
paragraphs: Compare pressure at the pump outlet with pressure at the irrigation zone where gauges are available. A large loss between those points can indicate pipe, filter or valve restrictions.

Confirm the water source can supply the pump continuously. Check valves, strainers and visible connections with the equipment isolated and safe to inspect. Electrical or internal pump repairs should be handled by a qualified technician.

sections.heading: Pressure is not the same as flow
paragraphs: A pump may show pressure while delivering too little flow, or deliver flow without enough pressure for the selected sprinkler or drip layout. Use the pump curve and system demand together; do not select a pump from horsepower alone.
Account for elevation, required operating pressure and friction losses in pipes, filters and fittings.

sections.heading: Information needed for pump selection

Required flow and number of irrigation zones
Elevation difference from source to field
Pipe diameter, material and approximate lengths
Required pressure at dripline or sprinkler
Power source and operating hours

sections.heading: Avoid replacing a pump by guesswork

description: Learn how to select an irrigation pump by flow, total head, water source, pressure, pipe losses, pump curve and power supply—not horsepower alone.
h1: How to choose the right irrigation pump
intro: The right irrigation pump must deliver the required flow at the total head of your system. A pump that looks powerful on its horsepower rating may still fail to provide the pressure and flow your sprinklers or drip zones need.

sections.heading: Start with the duty point: flow and total head
paragraphs: Flow is the volume of water delivered per unit time. Head represents the energy the pump must add to move water and overcome elevation, pipe friction, fittings and the pressure required at the irrigation equipment.
Calculate the required flow for the zone that will operate at one time. Then account for static lift or drawdown, elevation to the field, friction losses and required operating pressure.

sections.heading: Do not choose a pump by horsepower alone
paragraphs: Horsepower is not a complete pump-selection specification. Compare the manufacturer's pump curve with the required flow and head, and check the efficiency and operating range at that duty point.
A borehole pump also needs the borehole's sustainable yield and dynamic water level considered. Pumping beyond the source's capacity can cause water-level problems and damage.

sections.heading: Check the complete installation
bullets: Water source and dependable available flow
Required flow per irrigation zone
Total dynamic head and pressure at emitters or sprinklers
Pipe diameter, route length, elevation and friction losses
Pump curve, efficiency and motor requirements
Power source, controls, protection and maintenance access
Filtration, valves and any storage or pressure tank requirements

sections.heading: Common pump-selection mistakes
bullets: Buying the largest horsepower pump without hydraulic calculations
Ignoring elevation and pipe friction
Sizing for every zone when the system is designed to run zones separately—or vice versa
Assuming a pump's maximum flow and maximum head occur at the same time
Ignoring borehole yield, water quality or solar operating conditions
Failing to plan pressure gauges, protection and maintenance

paragraphs: Share the water source, water level or lift, distance to the field, elevation difference, pipe sizes, irrigation device and required operating zones. Existing pump model and performance details are helpful.

description: Practical irrigation dos and don'ts covering system design, pumps, filtration, dripline, sprinklers, installation, operation and maintenance in Kenya.
h1: Irrigation dos and don'ts for farms in Kenya
intro: Good irrigation depends on matching water delivery to the crop, soil, field and source. These practical checks help avoid preventable equipment problems and uneven watering; they do not replace a site-specific design or crop irrigation advice.

sections.heading: Do these things before buying
bullets: Measure the field and map crop rows, beds and elevations
Confirm dependable water availability and source quality
Check required flow and pressure for the irrigation devices
Plan filtration, flushing and maintenance access
Compare complete system scope—not only the pump or dripline price
Ask for a written equipment list, assumptions and installation scope

sections.heading: Avoid these common mistakes
bullets: Do not select a pump from horsepower or acreage alone
Do not assume every crop or soil needs the same emitter spacing or watering schedule
Do not operate all zones together unless the design and supply support it
Do not ignore filters, pressure regulation, flushing points or gauges
Do not mix pipe, fittings and components without checking size, pressure rating and compatibility
Do not leave leaks, clogged filters or damaged lines unattended
Do not fertilise through irrigation equipment without compatible products, correct setup and safe handling guidance

sections.heading: During installation and operation
paragraphs: Flush pipes and laterals before normal operation, test each zone and inspect for leaks or pressure differences. Keep records of operating times, maintenance and recurring faults.
Monitor soil moisture and crop response rather than relying only on a fixed timer. Irrigation frequency and duration vary with crop stage, soil, weather, system performance and water availability.

bullets: Water source has adequate supply

title: Solar vs Electric Irrigation Pumps in Kenya | DripTech
description: Compare solar and grid-powered irrigation pumps in Kenya by water demand, total head, energy availability, operating hours, storage, lifecycle cost and site constraints.
h1: Solar vs electric pumps for irrigation
intro: Solar and grid-powered pumps can both serve irrigation projects. The better option depends on the required flow and head, when water is needed, energy availability, storage, budget and maintenance—not simply the pump price.

sections.heading: When solar pumping may make sense
paragraphs: Solar pumping can be attractive where grid power is unavailable or unreliable and daytime water production can be matched to irrigation or storage. The design must use the pump curve and solar operating range for the required duty.

Cloud cover, season, panel orientation, shading, controller limits and water storage influence performance. Solar systems may need storage or a carefully planned irrigation schedule to bridge periods without pumping.

sections.heading: When grid-powered pumping may fit
paragraphs: Grid power can support predictable operating windows and may be practical where a reliable connection already exists. Energy costs, outages, electrical protection and installation conditions still need evaluation.
A grid pump should be selected for the actual duty point and motor supply. Electrical installation and protection should be handled by qualified personnel.

sections.heading: Compare the full system
bullets: Required flow and total dynamic head
Daily and seasonal water demand
Energy availability and reliability
Storage volume and timing of irrigation
Pump, controller, panels or electrical connection costs
Installation, protection, maintenance and replacement costs
Water source yield and pump operating limits

sections.heading: Avoid comparing only the purchase price
paragraphs: Compare lifecycle cost and delivered water under the expected operating conditions. A cheaper pump or power arrangement can become costly if it cannot meet the irrigation schedule or requires frequent intervention.
The water source, hydraulic design and crop demand should be confirmed before deciding between solar and grid power.

description: Use a practical irrigation startup checklist for flushing, filter checks, pressure readings, zone tests, leaks, pump protection and operator handover.
h1: Irrigation system startup and commissioning checklist
intro: A system should be checked before routine irrigation begins and after major repairs or upgrades. Commissioning confirms that components are installed correctly and that each zone operates within its intended conditions.

sections.heading: Before switching on
bullets: Confirm installation matches the approved layout and equipment schedule
Check valves, fittings, pipe supports and electrical protection
Confirm water source and pump operating limits
Ensure filters are installed and ready for cleaning
Identify zones, isolation valves and flushing points

sections.heading: Flush and inspect
paragraphs: Flush mainlines, submains and laterals in a controlled sequence according to the system design and component instructions. Keep flushing outlets accessible and avoid sending debris into emitters or sprinklers.
Inspect joints, filters, valves and end closures for leaks or blockages. Never exceed component pressure ratings during testing.

sections.heading: Test each zone
bullets: Run zones individually as designed
Record inlet and end-of-line pressure where measurement points exist
Check uniform operation and obvious dry or over-watered areas
Inspect sprinkler rotation/coverage or dripline discharge
Verify pump behaviour, controls and protection
Correct leaks, air issues, blockages or pressure problems before handover

sections.heading: Handover and maintenance records
paragraphs: Record equipment models, settings, pressure readings, zone sequence and maintenance tasks. Show operators how to start, stop, isolate, clean filters and report faults.
Commissioning results should be compared with the design and manufacturer specifications. Persistent deviations need investigation rather than simply increasing pump pressure.

description: Understand irrigation BOQs: pipes, dripline, filters, pumps, valves, fittings, quantities, specifications, installation and quotation assumptions.
h1: What should an irrigation bill of quantities include?
intro: An irrigation bill of quantities (BOQ) turns a design into a measurable equipment and work schedule. A useful BOQ describes items, sizes, specifications, quantities and scope so a customer can compare quotations more accurately.

sections.heading: Typical equipment schedule
bullets: Pumps and power/control equipment where applicable

Dripline, tape, emitters or sprinklers with relevant specifications
Filters, valves, regulators, gauges and flushing components
Fittings, connectors, reducers, tees, end closures and accessories

sections.heading: Quantities need a design basis
paragraphs: Pipe lengths should follow the layout and routing; dripline quantities follow the crop and bed arrangement; valves and fittings follow the zones and connections. Pump and filter specifications follow the hydraulic and water-quality requirements.
A BOQ based only on acreage or a generic kit can omit critical items or include unsuitable sizes. State assumptions, exclusions and any provisional quantities clearly.

title: Irrigation Zones Explained: Planning Flow & Pressure | Kenya
description: Learn how irrigation zones are planned using flow, pressure, field layout, crop needs, water supply and pump capacity.
h1: How irrigation zones are designed
intro: Irrigation zones divide a field into manageable sections that can be watered with the available flow and pressure. Good zoning helps control operating demand and makes troubleshooting and maintenance easier.

sections.heading: Why divide a farm into zones?
paragraphs: A water source or pump may not supply the entire field at the required flow and pressure simultaneously. Zones allow the system to operate sections in sequence and can account for differences in crop, terrain or equipment.
Zoning is not simply splitting acreage equally. The flow and pressure requirements of each zone should be compatible with the supply and hydraulic design.

sections.heading: Factors that affect zone layout
bullets: Emitter or sprinkler flow and spacing
Number of laterals or sprinklers operating together
Available pump flow and pressure at the duty point
Pipe diameters, route lengths and elevation
Crop blocks, soil differences and irrigation timing
Valve location, access, flushing and control requirements

sections.heading: Common zoning errors
bullets: Operating too many devices at once and losing pressure
Combining zones with very different hydraulic requirements without checking
Making zones difficult to isolate or maintain
Ignoring elevation changes and friction losses
Failing to label valves and document the operating sequence

sections.heading: What a zone schedule should show
paragraphs: A practical schedule identifies each zone, its area or crop block, expected flow, required operating pressure, control valve and sequence. These values should come from the system design and component specifications, not guesswork.

title: Irrigation Filter Selection by Water Source | Kenya
description: Choose irrigation filtration based on borehole, river, dam, tank or harvested water, emitter requirements and contamination risks.
h1: How to choose irrigation filtration for your water source
intro: Filtration protects irrigation equipment from particles that can clog emitters and sprinklers. The appropriate filter depends on the source, contaminant type, system flow and the irrigation device manufacturer's requirements.

sections.heading: Understand what is in the water
paragraphs: Borehole water may carry sand or other particles; surface water can contain silt, algae and organic debris; storage tanks can accumulate sediment. Water quality varies, so source labels alone do not determine the filter.

Where clogging or scaling is recurring, investigate the cause. Filtration removes suitable suspended material but does not automatically correct dissolved salts, chemical precipitation or biological growth.

sections.heading: Filter types and system checks
bullets: Screen filters for suitable particulate loads and straightforward cleaning
Disc filters where the contaminant profile and manufacturer guidance suit them
Media filtration for certain higher organic loads, designed and maintained correctly
Pre-filtration or multiple stages where source conditions require it
Filter mesh or micron rating compatible with emitter specifications
Flow capacity, pressure loss, cleaning method and maintenance access

sections.heading: Avoid these filtration mistakes
bullets: Do not select a filter by connection size alone
Do not use a finer rating without checking flow and pressure loss
Do not ignore filter cleaning frequency or differential pressure
Do not assume a filter solves dissolved mineral or chemical problems
Do not bypass filtration to compensate for a blocked or undersized unit

sections.heading: Design filtration into the system
paragraphs: A filtration plan should identify the water source, expected contaminants, flow per zone, filter specification, installation location, flushing or cleaning arrangement and maintenance instructions. Water testing may be needed for difficult sources or fertigation projects.

title: Gravity-Fed vs Pumped Irrigation in Kenya | DripTech
description: Compare gravity-fed and pumped irrigation by available elevation, pressure, flow, storage, field layout and operating requirements.
h1: Gravity-fed vs pumped irrigation: which suits your farm?
intro: Gravity-fed irrigation uses elevation to provide water pressure; pumped irrigation adds energy to meet flow and head requirements. Either approach must deliver the pressure and flow required by the irrigation equipment across the field.

sections.heading: When gravity supply may work
paragraphs: A raised tank or reservoir can provide pressure where its water level is sufficiently above the irrigated area and pipe losses are manageable. The usable pressure changes as tank level falls.
Gravity supply may simplify energy needs, but it still requires hydraulic checks, filtration, suitable valves and an adequate source/storage volume.

sections.heading: When pumping may be necessary
paragraphs: A pump may be required when source elevation, distance, field elevation or irrigation device pressure exceeds what gravity can provide. Pump selection should use the required flow and total head.
Pumping adds energy, equipment and maintenance considerations. The system should be designed around the actual operating duty, not maximum pump ratings alone.

sections.heading: Compare the full operating system
bullets: Available elevation and pressure at the field
Required flow and pressure per zone
Pipe route, diameter and friction losses
Water source yield and storage capacity
Energy supply, reliability and lifecycle cost
Filtration, controls, maintenance and expansion

sections.heading: Measure before choosing
paragraphs: Record the water level, field elevation, distance, pipe sizes and irrigation equipment specifications. A site-specific calculation can determine whether gravity is sufficient or pumping is required.

h1: Irrigation filtration systems and selection support in Kenya
intro: Correct filtration protects emitters and sprinkler nozzles from clogging. Filter selection depends on water source, suspended material, emitter requirements, flow and maintenance capacity—not a single filter size for every farm.

sections.heading: Filter types and selection considerations
paragraphs: Screen and disc filters are common for different particle loads; media filtration may be appropriate for water containing substantial organic material. sections.heading: Maintenance and troubleshooting
bullets: Monitor pressure difference across the filter
Flush or clean according to the manufacturer and water conditions
Inspect screens/discs and media condition
Flush lines and check emitters when clogging appears
Investigate water quality before repeatedly replacing components

paragraphs: Operate zones as specified by the design. Measure pressure and flow at designated points and compare readings with design values and equipment specifications. Never exceed component pressure ratings.
